claims.text: The initial equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy has a simple solid-solution structure.
Adding a controlled amount of carbon to CoCrFeNiTi can increase its strength.
Adding a controlled amount of carbon to CoCrFeNiTi can increase its hardness.
Carbon addition can retain the alloy's favorable plasticity.
Carbon addition can retain the alloy's favorable machinability.
Vacuum arc melting or mechanical alloying followed by heat treatment can produce a uniform distribution of carbon in the alloy.
Added carbon can form carbide precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Added carbon can dissolve in CoCrFeNiTi as a solid-solution strengthening solute.
Carbon-derived carbide precipitates obstruct dislocation movement.
Obstruction of dislocation movement by carbide precipitates increases alloy strength and hardness.
Dissolved carbon increases strength through solid-solution strengthening.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 20% greater hardness than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 20% greater strength than the unmodified alloy.
The predicted strength and hardness improvements will occur with minimal loss of plasticity.
The predicted strength and hardness improvements will occur with minimal loss of machinability.
The optimal carbon content and processing conditions are uncertain and require investigation.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires conditions permitting a simple solid-solution structure, whereas one proposed mediator is formation of carbide precipitates, which would make the modified microstructure multiphase unless the boundary is intended to describe only the starting alloy.
